facts: The `prefs` parameter is attacker-controlled (@RequestParam) — observed at ReportPrefsController.java:31.
The bytes are passed to ObjectInputStream.readObject() with no ObjectInputFilter and no resolveClass() override — observed at line 33-34.
The cast to ReportPreferences happens AFTER readObject() returns — observed at line 34.
conclusions: Because the cast is post-deserialization, arbitrary classes are instantiated before any type check, so the ReportPreferences type does not constrain what is deserialized.
Whether this reaches full RCE depends on the presence of a usable gadget chain among the service's transitive dependencies.
hypotheses: A commons-collections / spring-core style gadget is likely reachable given a typical Spring Boot classpath, but this has NOT been confirmed against this project's exact dependency tree.

threat.actor: Unauthenticated remote caller who can POST to the endpoint.
preconditions: A usable gadget chain on the classpath (for RCE); none needed for DoS
threat.attacker_input: A base64-encoded, crafted Java serialized object graph in the `prefs` parameter.
threat.violated_property: Integrity of code execution (untrusted data must not become executable object graphs).
threat.availability_impact: High (deserialization bombs cause CPU/memory exhaustion without any gadget)
threat.attack_narrative: Attacker crafts a serialized payload -> sends it as `prefs` -> ObjectInputStream reconstructs the attacker's object graph -> gadget chain executes during readObject()/finalize -> code runs in the report-service process, before the ReportPreferences cast is ever evaluated.

security_objective: Untrusted, client-supplied bytes must NEVER drive native Java object reconstruction: after remediation it must be impossible for a request to cause instantiation of any class the endpoint did not explicitly intend, and impossible to invoke gadget behaviour during parsing.

candidates.approach: Stop using native Java serialization on the wire. Accept the preferences as JSON bound to the ReportPreferences DTO (e.g. @RequestBody with Jackson, default typing DISABLED), and delete the ObjectInputStream path entirely.
candidates.security_mechanism: Format change to a non-executable data format with no polymorphic type resolution — untrusted input can only populate fields of one known DTO, never choose classes.
advantages: Eliminates the root cause rather than filtering it — there is no readObject() sink left to attack.
No gadget chain is reachable because no arbitrary class instantiation occurs.
Aligns with the rest of the codebase, which already uses JSON DTOs (e.g. EmployeeResponse).
limitations: Breaks wire compatibility with any existing client that sends the serialized token — those clients must be updated to send JSON.
bypass_risks: Only if Jackson polymorphic/default typing is later enabled (that would reintroduce a CWE-502-class hole) — must be explicitly kept off.
validation_requirements: A JSON body binds to ReportPreferences and applies correctly.
A native serialized payload is now rejected as malformed JSON, not deserialized.

candidates.approach: If the native serialization wire format MUST be preserved, keep ObjectInputStream but install a strict allow-list ObjectInputFilter (JEP 290) that permits only ReportPreferences (+ its required JDK value types) and rejects everything else, with a small maxdepth/maxrefs budget.
candidates.security_mechanism: Deserialization allow-list (ObjectInputFilter) — resolveClass is constrained so only the intended class graph can be reconstructed; a resource budget blocks deserialization bombs.
advantages: Preserves the existing wire format and clients.
Blocks gadget chains because gadget classes are not on the allow-list.
Resource limits also address the DoS vector.
limitations: Allow-list must be maintained; an over-broad pattern silently re-opens the hole.
Still native serialization — riskier and harder to reason about than a data format.
bypass_risks: A too-permissive filter pattern (e.g. allowing a whole package) can still admit a gadget.
Filter applies to this stream only; any other ObjectInputStream added later is unprotected unless a JVM-wide filter is set.
behavioral_risks: Legitimate but unlisted nested types would be rejected — the allow-list must be complete.
validation_requirements: A payload referencing any non-allow-listed class is rejected before instantiation.
A deep/over-large payload is rejected by the resource budget.

evaluation.other_entrypoints: none — the only readObject() is here
evaluation.new_weakness: none if default typing stays off
evaluation.simpler_safer_alt: this IS the simplest safe option

evaluation.other_entrypoints: future ObjectInputStreams unprotected unless JVM-wide filter

recommendation.why_selected: It removes the root cause entirely — with no readObject() sink there is nothing left to attack — and it is the smallest change that fully restores the security objective while matching the codebase's existing JSON-DTO convention.
recommendation.why_alternatives_rejected: CAND-002 only constrains the sink rather than removing it, depends on an allow-list that silently re-opens the hole if mis-maintained, and leaves native deserialization (and any future ObjectInputStream) as ongoing risk. It is the right fallback ONLY if the serialized wire format cannot be changed.
recommendation.security_property_restored: Untrusted input can no longer cause instantiation of arbitrary classes; it can only populate the fields of one known DTO.
recommendation.expected_behavior_after: Preferences are submitted as JSON and applied exactly as before; previously-valid serialized tokens are rejected as malformed input.
known_limitations: Existing clients sending the old serialized token must migrate to JSON.
recommendation.residual_risk: Low, provided Jackson default/polymorphic typing is never enabled on this path. This is a novel, internally-derived recommendation and must be human-reviewed before implementation.

validation_requirements.assertion: A valid JSON preferences body binds to ReportPreferences and is applied.
A native Java serialized payload in `prefs` is no longer deserialized (rejected as invalid input).
A known deserialization-bomb / gadget payload produces no class instantiation and no code execution.
Malformed JSON is rejected with a 4xx, not processed.
Existing legitimate preference values continue to apply unchanged when sent as JSON.
No ObjectInputStream.readObject() on request-derived bytes remains in the module (SAST/grep gate).

provenance.reasoning: Internally derived from the vulnerability evidence and established secure-coding principles for CWE-502 (avoid native deserialization of untrusted data; prefer a non-executable data format; if unavoidable, allow-list via ObjectInputFilter). No external documentation was retrievable in this runtime, so NO external citation is claimed and confidence is Low.
